analysis.one_liner: Requires schools to use least-toxic pest control and notify parents before spraying pesticides.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Senator Torricelli with no cosponsors, never got a hearing or vote; it died in the Senate Agriculture Committee when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended the nation's pesticide law to require every public school to adopt an integrated pest management system — a program that favors sanitation, repairs, and other nonchemical methods, and allows only 'least toxic' pesticides after those options are exhausted. Schools could not spray or fog pesticides while buildings were in use, and would have to give parents and staff 72 hours' notice and posted warnings before using any stronger pesticide, with emergency exceptions. It created a national advisory board to write standards, an EPA office to coordinate school pest management, grants to help school districts comply, and up to $10,000 civil penalties for violations. The bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee on the day it was introduced and never received any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Children in public schools and their parents, along with teachers and school staff, gain protection from pesticide exposure. Asthma and cancer are the bill's stated concerns: its findings cite rising childhood asthma and cancer rates and note children are more susceptible to pesticides than adults. Parents gain a right to know in advance what chemicals will be used in their children's classrooms and on playgrounds, and school employees gain whistleblower-style protection from retaliation for reporting violations.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every school district to implement an integrated pest management system that uses inspections, monitoring, sanitation, structural repair, and biological controls, turning to least-toxic pesticides only after nonchemical methods are exhausted.
Bars pesticide application while a school building or ground is occupied and blocks use of a treated area for 24 hours after application of anything other than a least-toxic pesticide.

Requires 72 hours' advance notice to every parent, guardian, and staff member before any non-least-toxic pesticide is used, including the pesticide's name, location, timing, and potential adverse effects, plus posted warning signs at every entrance.
Prohibits schools from discriminating against employees who report violations or refuse to apply pesticides unlawfully, with reinstatement and back pay as remedies.
Authorizes federal grants to school districts, appropriated at $7 million per year for fiscal years 2000 through 2004, to help develop and implement the pest management systems.

analysis.who_pays: Conventional pesticide manufacturers and professional applicators would lose a school market: within six years, only pesticides on the federal 'least toxic' list could be used in schools unless the EPA met the bill's deadlines. School districts would bear new administrative duties — designating a contact person, keeping pesticide use records open to the public, and sending annual notices — though the bill authorizes $7 million a year in federal grants to offset compliance costs.

drawbacks.text: School districts would take on real administrative burdens: designating a trained contact person in every district, maintaining pesticide use records and safety data sheets for public review, and issuing detailed 72-hour notices for every application, and the $7 million in annual grants may not cover the full cost.

A blanket restriction on all but 'least toxic' pesticides could leave schools with fewer options against serious infestations, though the bill preserves emergency application without prior notice when a pest threatens a student's or staff member's health or safety, followed by next-day notification.

The bill layered a new advisory board, a new EPA office, technical advisory panels, and a six-year regulatory process on top of existing pesticide registration, which critics could reasonably call an unusually heavy apparatus for a single school setting.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — children, parents, and staff knowing what chemicals are used in schools and sharply reducing exposure to the more hazardous ones — is substantial and directly tied to the health of a vulnerable population. The costs are real but ordinary for a regulatory program: paperwork for school districts, compliance adjustments for pest-control companies, and a shift in the school pesticide market toward lower-toxicity products. The main design weakness is bureaucratic complexity — multiple boards, panels, and deadlines — rather than any cost borne by families.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee the day it was introduced in February 2000, got no hearing, no markup, and no vote, and expired when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Senator Robert Torricelli introduced the School Environment Protection Act of 1999 on February 28, 2000; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry the same day.
The bill had zero cosponsors, and the only action in its entire history was its introduction and committee referral.

The bill would have required schools to adopt integrated pest management, restricted pesticide use in schools to least-toxic products within six years, and given parents and staff 72-hour notice before any stronger pesticide application.
The 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001, and the bill was never taken up again; a bill that does not advance past committee by the end of a Congress dies and must be reintroduced from scratch.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers of conventional pesticides and school pest-control contractors kept the status quo: no federal requirement to notify parents or shift to least-toxic products in schools. Schoolchildren and their parents gained nothing, and Senator Torricelli's bill died with no cosponsors or committee action.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Conventional pesticide makers and status quo pest control

for.name: Sen. Robert Torricelli
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate on February 28, 2000.

against.name: Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and never reported it, held a hearing, or scheduled action on it.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill attracted no cosponsors from either party, so the record shows only a single Democratic sponsor and no visible partisan lineup.

industries.note: The bill barred, within six years, any pesticide not on a federal least-toxic list from use in schools, and required the EPA to review pesticides used in schools for cancer, reproductive, neurological, and endocrine effects. That would shrink the school market for conventional products; the industry's interest in keeping them available ran against the bill's child-health purpose.

The bill's notification, posting, and integrated-management requirements would change how applicators work in schools, but the bill also seated a pest-control trade organization on its advisory board and IPM programs create demand for trained inspection and nonchemical services.

Districts would face new duties — a designated contact person, public pesticide-use records, annual notices — but receive $7 million a year in federal grants and gain a framework that reduces chemical use in their own buildings.
